items.title: Remove three quarters of a liver and it grows back
items.claim: Humans can lose 70-75% of their liver (in surgery or donation) and regrow it to original size within weeks. The liver is the only solid human organ with this level of regenerative ability. Even other strongly regenerative tissues (skin, bone marrow) can't grow back this much organ.

options.text: A reservoir of liver stem cells expands

Mature hepatocytes (normally quiescent) re-enter the cell cycle and divide; growth factors (HGF, EGF, IL-6) signal the remaining cells to proliferate until the original organ mass is restored, then stop
Surrounding organs grow into the missing space
The bile duct generates new liver tissue

items.reveal:
Normal adult liver: hepatocytes (~80% of liver cells) sit in G0, dividing at most once every year or two. Cellular workhorses doing biochemistry, not growing.

After partial hepatectomy (surgical removal): within hours, growth factors (hepatocyte growth factor HGF, EGF, TGF-alpha) surge in the portal blood. Hepatocytes enter S phase by 24-48 hours, divide, and continue dividing until liver mass returns. Then they switch off and resume their quiescent state.

Full regeneration in 2-3 weeks. Donors who give part of their liver for transplant recover their original liver mass and function.

Limit: the regeneration requires intact liver remnant. Cirrhotic livers — where hepatocytes have been replaced by scar tissue — cannot regenerate. Acute liver failure with widespread cell death may also overwhelm the regenerative response.

The Prometheus myth (vulture eats his liver, which regrows nightly) suggests ancient Greek anatomists may have noticed liver regeneration. Modern molecular understanding mostly dates from the 1980s-90s.

The liver's regenerative capacity is one of the foundations of living donor transplants — a partial donation to a recipient leaves both with functional livers.
items.why: Major organ regrowth seems out of reach for mammals. The liver does it routinely — and the molecular signals are now well enough understood to be co-opted for transplant medicine.

items.title: Your mitochondria used to be a separate organism
items.claim: Mitochondria have their own DNA, their own ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide independently of the cell. About 2 billion years ago, a free-living alpha-proteobacterium got engulfed by another cell and stayed.
items.prompt: What's the strongest evidence mitochondria were once independent?

options.text: They are smaller than the host cell

Mitochondrial DNA is circular (like a bacterial chromosome), their ribosomes resemble bacterial ribosomes (and are inhibited by antibiotics like chloramphenicol), and their inner membrane has bacteria-like lipid composition

items.reveal_title: Lynn Margulis and the endosymbiotic theory
items.reveal:
Lynn Margulis proposed in 1967 that mitochondria descend from free-living alpha-proteobacteria, and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria. Her paper was rejected fifteen times before being accepted. The orthodoxy disliked the idea of major evolution happening by merger rather than gradual modification.

The evidence accumulated:
- Circular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
- Bacterial-style ribosomes; sensitive to bacterial antibiotics.
- Double membranes (the outer from the host cell, the inner from the bacterium).
- Replication by binary fission, independent of cell division.
- Phylogenetic analysis: mitochondrial genes group with Rickettsia (intracellular alpha-proteobacteria).

All eukaryotes (including animals, plants, fungi) descend from this single ancient merger. Without it, complex life wouldn't exist.
items.why: Evolution is taught as branching divergence. Some of the most important steps came from merger — two organisms becoming one.

items.title: Your liver and your eyes have separate clocks
items.claim: Every cell in your body has its own molecular clock. The 'master' clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) synchronises them. Eating at the wrong time can desynchronise organs from each other — same as jet lag without the travel.
items.prompt: What is a cellular circadian clock made of?

options.text: A transcription-translation feedback loop: genes (BMAL1/CLOCK in mammals) drive expression of inhibitor proteins (PER, CRY) that themselves repress the original genes — the cycle takes about 24 hours to complete
An internal sundial of pigment molecules

items.reveal:
In Drosophila, Hall, Rosbash and Young identified Period (PER) gene and worked out the negative feedback loop: PER protein accumulates in the cell, eventually shuts down its own transcription, then degrades, allowing the cycle to repeat. Mammals have BMAL1/CLOCK driving PER1/2/3 and CRY1/2, with the same logic.

The cycle's intrinsic period is close to 24 hours; light input (via melanopsin in retinal ganglion cells) synchronises it to the day.

Peripheral clocks (in liver, muscle, fat) entrain primarily to feeding times. Eating at midnight tells your liver it's daytime even as your SCN says it's night — exactly the desynchronisation seen in shift workers, who have elevated rates of metabolic disease and some cancers.
items.why: The biological clock is pictured as one master organ. Every cell has one, and keeping them aligned is a daily ongoing process — and easily disrupted.
